questions.question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth merchant in Delft, built his microscopes with just one glass lens, set in a small brass plate. The compound microscopes of his day, such as Robert Hooke's, had two lenses in a tube, yet Leeuwenhoek's showed far finer detail. Why did one lens do better than two?
questions.answer: The lenses of the day blurred, and each extra lens added blur
choices: The lenses of the day blurred, and each extra lens added blur
A second lens undoes much of the magnifying of the first
His single lens was much larger than the lenses in a tube
His single lens magnified less, which kept the picture sharp
questions.context: Every lens of the time blurred the image a little and fringed its edges with colour, and a compound microscope's two lenses added their flaws together; Hooke himself admitted that a single lens showed some things more distinctly. Leeuwenhoek's lenses were tiny, most under 3 millimetres across, because the smaller a microscope lens is, the more it magnifies: his best magnified over 250 times, while Hooke's magnified up to about 50. Two lenses never undo each other's work; in a compound microscope their powers multiply.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade histories of cell theory open with Leeuwenhoek's single-lens microscopes, and why they beat the compound microscopes of his day is the unit's plainest case of a better tool changing what could be known.

questions.question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek scraped a little white matter, as thick as batter, from between his teeth in 1683. He mixed it with pure rainwater, and through his lens he saw many tiny living things moving about in it. What were they?
questions.context: The tiny living things from his teeth were bacteria, and his letter of 17 September 1683 is often cited as the first clear sighting of them; his Dutch word for such creatures meant little animals, which his English translators turned into animalcules. The rainwater held none of them, so they had to come from his teeth. Viruses are far too small for any lens like his, and mites and worms are many-celled animals, far bigger than the single cells he saw.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade cell-theory histories credit Leeuwenhoek with the first sight of bacteria, and the matter scraped from his own teeth is the classic case.

questions.question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek wrote to the Royal Society in London in 1676 that one drop of pepper water held more than a million living creatures, all far too small for the eye. Some of the Fellows doubted him. What would give them the strongest evidence that he was right?
questions.answer: A Fellow seeing them for himself through his own microscope
choices: A Fellow seeing them for himself through his own microscope
Eight respected men of Delft vouching that they saw them
Careful drawings of the creatures made by Leeuwenhoek
A longer letter from Leeuwenhoek counting them drop by drop
questions.context: Witnesses, drawings and counts all depended on Leeuwenhoek and his own lenses, and he would not explain his methods; an observation that someone else repeats does not depend on him. The Society asked Robert Hooke to build a microscope strong enough, and in November 1677, after two failures, Hooke saw 'great numbers of exceedingly small animals swimming to and fro' before Christopher Wren and other Fellows. The minutes record that there was then no longer any doubt of Leeuwenhoek's discovery.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders learn to judge a claim by the strength of its evidence and the methods behind it (TEKS 6.4A-B in the map), and the Royal Society's repeat of Leeuwenhoek's observation is the classic case of a claim checked.

questions.question: Plant cells stand out clearly under a microscope, each boxed in by a thick wall, and Matthias Schleiden argued in 1838 that every plant is built of them. Animal cells have no wall, so their edges are harder to see. Yet Theodor Schwann showed in 1839 that animals are built of cells too. What did he look for to pick out each cell?
questions.context: Schleiden held the nucleus to be the most important part of a cell, and when the two men talked about nuclei, Schwann remembered seeing similar structures in animal cells; he reasoned that if plants and animals were built alike, the nucleus should turn up in animal tissue too, and his microscope found nuclei in tissue after tissue. Animal cells have no chloroplasts, the cytoplasm fills all the space around the nucleus and gives no single spot to look for, and mitochondria were not described until 1857.
questions.grade_note: Schleiden for plants and Schwann for animals are the names 6th-grade units give for how cell theory was built, and the nucleus Schwann followed ties the story to the cell parts the grade learns.

questions.question: Robert Remak watched red blood cells in chicken embryos split in two, and in 1852 he published his evidence that new cells come from cells that divide. Few took notice. Three years later another scientist made the idea famous in four Latin words meaning 'every cell from a cell', without naming Remak. Who was he?
questions.context: Rudolf Virchow, a German doctor who had at first doubted that cells divide, made the Latin motto omnis cellula e cellula famous in 1855; his essay never named Remak, and the historian Paul Weindling says Virchow plagiarised Remak's idea. Schleiden and Schwann had thought that new cells form out of a fluid, as crystals do. Louis Pasteur's flasks of broth, a few years later, tested where microbes come from, not how cells are made.
questions.grade_note: Virchow's 'every cell from a cell' is the usual last step of the 6th-grade cell-theory story, and Remak's earlier evidence, now often credited with it, tells that step honestly.

questions.question: Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll built a new kind of microscope in Berlin in 1931. It aims a beam of electrons, not light, at its sample, and it shows far finer detail than any light microscope can. What tiny things, most of them too small for any light microscope, did it let scientists see clearly for the first time?
questions.context: Most viruses are about a hundredth the size of a bacterium, too small for any light microscope, and the first pictures of the tobacco mosaic virus came from an electron microscope in 1939. Bacteria, cell nuclei and chloroplasts are all big enough to see with a light microscope, and Leeuwenhoek saw bacteria more than 250 years earlier.
questions.grade_note: Middle-school cell units set the light microscope beside the electron microscope, and the viruses it first showed are the plainest case of a new tool revealing what no older one could.

questions.question: A girl lays a thin slice of onion skin on a slide under her school microscope. So much light comes up through it that the pale cells look washed out and are hard to make out. Which part of the microscope should she adjust?
questions.context: The diaphragm, under the stage, opens and closes to let more or less light up through the slide, and closing it a little cuts the glare and makes pale cells stand out. The fine focus knob sharpens the picture, the eyepiece is the lens the eye looks through, and the stage clips only hold the slide in place.
questions.grade_note: The parts of a light microscope and the job each does are standard 6th-grade lab content, taught before students look at cells.

questions.question: A boy finds an onion cell with the low-power objective lens of his microscope, then turns the nosepiece to bring the high-power lens over the slide. Why should he now focus with only the fine focus knob, never the coarse one?
questions.answer: The coarse knob could crash the lens into the slide
choices: The coarse knob could crash the lens into the slide
The coarse knob would change the lens's power again
The coarse knob moves the slide only from side to side
The coarse knob dims the light too much to see by
questions.context: The coarse knob makes big moves, right for finding a cell at low power, but the high-power lens sits very close to the slide, and one big turn can scratch the lens and crack the slide. The fine knob makes the small moves high power needs. Focusing moves the lens and slide closer or farther apart and never changes the magnification.
questions.grade_note: Focusing with the coarse knob at low power and only the fine knob at high power is a standard 6th-grade microscope lab rule, and its reason is the job of each knob.

questions.question: A student's school microscope has an eyepiece lens marked 10x and a high-power objective lens, the one just above the slide, marked 40x. She looks at a slide of cheek cells with the high-power lens. How does she work out how many times bigger the cells look?
questions.context: The objective makes a picture of the cells 40 times bigger, and the eyepiece enlarges that picture 10 times more, so the total magnification is the product of the two: 10 times 40 is 400. Adding the two would give only 50, and either number alone leaves out one of the two lenses the light passes through.
questions.grade_note: Working out total magnification from the eyepiece and the objective is a standard 6th-grade microscope skill, and adding the two numbers is the usual slip.

638826d093.why: Judge (medium): 'pure rainwater' ruled out Algae, so 'Algae' is now 'Tiny worms', a many-celled animal of the old tooth-worm kind. The stem's last sentence ('the first clear report of their kind') was cut, since only a newly seen kind of creature fits it. Fact-check error fixed in the card: Leeuwenhoek wrote in Dutch (dierken, diertgens), and 'animalcules' is his English translators' word; the card also says why mites and worms are wrong (F34, F35).

a27387fc4c.why: Judge (medium): the plant and animal contrast left two plant-only parts dead, so 'Its central vacuole' is now 'Its cytoplasm', a part every animal cell has but no landmark (F36). Judge (low): the closer now asks what he looked for to pick out each cell; 'easy to pick out' in the first sentence became 'stand out clearly' so the phrase is not used twice, and 'found cells all through animal tissue' was cut for length.

460982845a.why: Judge (medium): the old key (cells split in two) asked the same fact as the pilot cells unit's scraped-knee question. Re-keyed, as the judge proposed, on who made 'every cell from a cell' famous: Virchow, whom no unit asks about. Remak's evidence still comes first and Virchow is said to have left him out, with the plagiarism charge put in Paul Weindling's mouth. Judge (low): the card no longer says Virchow 'got the credit', only that he made the motto famous (Raspail wrote it first).

21c410c1d7.why: Judge (medium): 'how many times bigger ... through both lenses together' ruled out the two 'alone' choices. Used the judge's second fix: the stem now gives only the marks on the lenses, so taking the objective's number alone (the lens she has just turned to) stays a live slip. The judge's first fix (ask why the powers multiply) was not used: two of its wrong choices (the eyepiece gathers light, it moves the cell nearer) fall to common sense once the stem says the eyepiece makes things look bigger. The card now gives the why: the eyepiece enlarges the picture the objective has already made (F38).
